items.title: U.S. and German scientists win Nobel Price in medicine for discoveries on optogenetics
items.standfirst: American Karl Deisseroth, a neuroscientist and psychiatrist, has won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, along with two German scientists. Their discoveries in optogenetics could reshape how we study the brain and understand how it processes information. Dr. Heather Berlin, an associate professor of psychiatry and neuroscience at Mount Sinai, joins CBS News to discuss.

items.title: Switching on brain cells: the Nobel-winning science of optogenetics
items.standfirst: The Nobel medicine prize was awarded Monday to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their pioneering work in the neuroscience field of optogenetics. In optogenetics, scientists control neurones by stimulating them with light -- potentially unlocking breakthroughs for conditions such as dementia, depression and blindness. FRANCE 24's Monte Francis reports.

clusters.title: Spain’s Leader Is Betting His Government on the Housing Crisis
clusters.neutral_headline: Spain’s Leader Is Betting His Government on the Housing Crisis

items.title: Spain’s Leader Is Betting His Government on the Housing Crisis
items.standfirst: The Spanish Prime Minister called for early elections after his governing coalition was unable to pass a package of emergency housing measures.
items.content: The Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sanchez, sits during a plenary session of the Congress of Deputies in Madrid on Oct. 2, 2026. —Eduardo Parra—Europa Press/Getty ImagesPrime Minister Pedro Sánchez of Spain called for early elections on Monday after Parliament last week rejected two key housing decrees amid widespread protests over rising rents and housing scarcity. The elections, originally scheduled to take place next summer, will now be held on Nov. 29.One of the decrees was a relief package aiming to extend eviction protections for vulnerable households, regulate rentals, and offer tax relief and assistance for renters, landlords, and first-time homebuyers, while the other aimed to offer greater stability for renters by establishing automatic renewals. The rejected measures came from Sánchez’s governing coalition, comprising his Socialist Party, PSOE, and the left-wing alliance Sumar. The coalition lacks a majority in Parliament and must rely on other parties to pass legislation. That dependence leaves the government vulnerable when those parties withhold their support—which is what played out with the two housing measures on Oct. 2.In calling early elections, Sánchez is hoping voters will give his coalition enough support in Parliament to advance its housing agenda—but risks handing his opponents the majority instead. “To do more, we need to renew and expand the people’s support,” Sánchez said in a statement on Monday. But he faces a central challenge: persuading voters to blame the parties that blocked his proposals, rather than his government, for the lack of relief.Various parties have offered differing explanations for why they rejected the decrees. Junts—a Catalan pro-independence party—said in a statement Oct. 1 that many of the proposed measures would reduce the supply of rental homes and drive up prices, making housing even harder to access for people with lower incomes. Juan Bravo, housing spokesman for the conservative PP party, said on Oct. 2 that the government was proposing significant market interventions without adequately addressing the shortage of homes through construction.Sergio Nasarre Aznar, a professor of civil law at Universitat Rovira i Virgili, agrees with some of the points the parties have made in opposing the decrees, telling TIME that “what Pedro Sánchez is proposing will cause a serious breakdown of the housing market”—making it even more difficult to access housing. He also argues that the measures could make housing harder to access by increasing legal uncertainty. He warns of “the threat of future court rulings annulling some of the measures.”Sánchez’s opponents are also choosing to emphasize other issues, including immigration: Vox leader Santiago Abascal, for instance, has made tougher migration policies a condition of supporting a future government with the conservative PP.The move is also a gamble because Sánchez’s party may need to overcome blowback over corruption scandals, its handling of migration, and repeated difficulty securing support in Parliament.Pablo Simón, a political scientist with the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, tells TIME that focusing on housing could help Sánchez move beyond those difficulties and engage progressive voters.“After months dominated by corruption scandals, parliamentary weakness, and government fatigue, housing gives Sánchez an issue around which he believes he may be able to mobilize key parts of the progressive electorate again,” he says, “particularly younger voters, renters and voters in large cities.”How did housing become the breaking point? Spain’s housing supply has struggled to keep pace with demand in recent years, and an increasingly unaffordable market has become a growing pressure point, with the Bank of Spain showing an estimated housing shortfall of 750,000 homes accumulating from 2021 to 2025. The Spanish Youth Council’s 2025 report showed an average monthly rent of €1,176, the equivalent of roughly $1,317, which then represented 98.7% of a young person’s average salary in Spain. But public outrage came to a head in September when an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid after occupying the unit for decades. Thousands of protestors took to the streets.Simón believes that the Prime Minister sees their fury as an opportunity.“Sánchez is taking advantage of what is probably the best window of opportunity available to minimize PSOE losses,” he says. “If he manages to make the campaign revolve around this issue, he could hope to close the gap with the PP and, in the most favourable scenario for him, even compete to finish as the largest party.”That does not mean Sánchez expects to win an outright majority, Simón cautions. And he further questions if housing can become a decisive voting issue.“It is clearly one of Spain's most important social problems and has a strong capacity to generate political mobilization, but that does not necessarily mean it will determine how people vote,” he says.What is at stake in the election?With a snap election, Sánchez is gambling that the housing issue will remobilize the left and give his coalition more seats in Parliament to advance its proposals. But even if the Prime Minister succeeds in putting housing at the center of the campaign, Simón says, “that does not automatically mean that the PSOE will be the party that benefits electorally from it.”The PP, Vox and Junts could still hold enough seats between them to block Sánchez’s housing proposals, he says, noting that far-right Vox is “growing strongly.”Politico polling from Sept. 26 shows Sánchez entering the election campaign at a disadvantage, with PP at 34% of the vote share next to PSOE’s 26%. Vox follows at 18%, while Sumar holds some 5%. Those figures predate the election announcement and do not directly predict parliamentary seats.“It is widely assumed that the right-wing bloc will secure an absolute majority,” Simón says, “so the main question is not whether Sánchez can remain in government, but how much he can limit the scale of the defeat.”A defeat for Sánchez could have consequences beyond its borders. A government led by the conservative PP, potentially with far-right Vox, would reinforce Europe’s shift to the right, alongside conservative-led Germany and far-right-led Italy. It could also remove a prominent progressive voice from European debates over immigration, defense spending, and relations with Israel.If Sánchez secures the greater parliamentary support he’s seeking, meanwhile, it would not guarantee relief from rising housing costs.Previous efforts illustrate the difficulties. Spain’s 2023 housing law enabled rent limits in designated high-pressure areas, but implementation has varied by region. Attempts to tighten rules on temporary rentals have also encountered parliamentary resistance. A subsequent rental-regulation proposal advanced in December 2024, showing that negotiations could overcome some divisions. But support for debating the legislation did not mean agreement on its substance. At the same time, expanding public housing requires years of investment and cooperation between national and regional authorities. A new parliamentary majority would not, on its own, remove those obstacles. And Simón says it remains unclear which party can claim ownership of the housing issue.“Voters assign responsibility to different levels of government, and there is no broad consensus on the appropriate solutions,” he explains. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative PP, said on Monday that he believes Sánchez called the election out of fear—but he supports the decision. "These are not elections like the previous ones: This is about Spain defeating Sánchez and what he represents,” he said. He acknowledged the housing crisis has yet to be addressed, claiming that “the cost of living is unbearable” in Spain and that “housing is out of reach.”Vox leader Abascal commented on Monday that focusing on “national priority, deregulation, and remigration” would be the conditions for a potential governing alliance with the PP.What is the process of calling for a snap election in Spain?Following Sánchez’s announcement, elections are set to take place Nov. 29. The call for early elections is fairly common and reflects a core element of Spain’s electoral process.Spain’s Constitution allows the prime minister, after consulting the Cabinet, to seek the early dissolution of Parliament and a new election. The king formally issues the decree; however, this action is a formality. Sánchez’s office said Monday that King Felipe VI’s election decree would be published Tuesday. The previous election was July 23, 2023, and parliamentary terms normally last four years, meaning that the latest possible date to hold elections would have been Aug. 22, 2027. No official date had been set when Sánchez called to move up the timeline by as many as nine months. Sánchez has called early elections before: in 2019, after Parliament rejected his budget, and in 2023, after his party suffered losses in local and regional elections. The PP won the most seats in the July 2023 vote, but Sánchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to remain Prime Minister.

items.title: Sanchez chose 'best moment in a sea of troubles' to call for snap election, analyst says
items.standfirst: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday called an early election for November 29, aiming to increase his parliamentary support after lawmakers last week rejected proposals to address a housing crisis that has drawn nationwide protests. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Mark Owen, Javier Carbonell, Policy Analyst at the European Policy Centre, explains that Sanchez has chosen "the best moment in a sea of troubles" to call snap elections as he is likely to capitalise on the mobilisation of left-wing voters during the housing protests.

items.standfirst: Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surgeFlávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot. Continue reading...

items.title: Suspected Chinese Foreign Agent Arrested at Los Angeles Airport
items.standfirst: The suspect, a 34-year-old from California, was allegedly conducting surveillance on the Taiwanese President’s family.
items.content: A screenshot from a video of authorities arresting a Chinese national suspected of acting on behalf of the Chinese government, posted by First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli on X on Oct. 4, 2026. —Screenshot from @USAttyEssayliThe FBI arrested a suspected Chinese foreign agent at the Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday after she allegedly surveilled the Taiwanese President’s family.Bill Essayli, the First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, posted on social media platform X that FBI agents in Los Angeles nabbed 34-year-old Wanying “Heather” Zhang of Irvine, Calif., as she was attempting to depart for China.Zhang was arrested on a federal complaint charging her with acting as an unregistered Chinese agent, Essayli said. She is slated to appear in federal court in Los Angeles Monday.FBI Director Kash Patel appeared to laud the arrest on social media. “Foreign adversaries take note: America is no longer a safe place to run your espionage operations,” Patel wrote. “Allegedly surveil a foreign leader’s family on U.S. soil for [China]—and try to catch a flight back to Shanghai? Not happening.”A spokesperson for Taiwan’s presidential office described on Monday Zhang’s purported actions as a “classic case of transnational repression” and thanked the U.S. government.“Our country expresses ​the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of ​nations,” the spokesperson said.Taiwan, the self-governing island that China claims to have sovereignty over, has been a point of contention between Washington and Beijing for decades. Washington, while acknowledging Beijing’s position on Taiwan, has maintained close unofficial relations with Taipei, though those ties have been mired in uncertainty under U.S. President Donald Trump. China, meanwhile, has long branded Taiwan’s leader William Lai Ching-te as a separatist and a “destroyer of peace.”During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s recent state visit to the U.S., President Trump said of the topic: “We didn’t spend a lot of time talking about Taiwan.”Zhang’s arrest comes months after Eileen Wang, a former mayor of Arcadia, Calif., pleaded guilty to acting as an illegal agent for the Chinese government. The former mayor admitted to promoting pro-Beijing content in the U.S. Both cases are part of a reported pattern of people acting on behalf of the Chinese government to target Chinese dissidents outside of China.While the American public’s view of China has improved, and even as Beijing makes diplomatic overtures to the Trump Administration, many in Washington remain hawkish against the U.S.’s geopolitical rival. The latest report from the U.S. Congressional-Executive Commission on China continues to warn about Beijing’s transnational repression activities, including intimidation and the targeting of Hong Kongers, Uyghurs, Tibetans, Taiwanese figures, and other Chinese dissidents.Sen. Rick Scott (R, Fla.) posted on X: “This is only further PROOF of what we already know—they’re actively infiltrating our country and threatening our national security.”What U.S. authorities are allegingAuthorities filed a criminal complaint against Zhang in federal court, CBS News and Fox News reported, with an affidavit from an FBI special agent. According to a copy of the 27-page complaint Fox News obtained, Zhang, who previously attended a university in Beijing and was a registered real estate agent in Southern California, was allegedly in contact with at least two individuals apparently working for the Chinese government. Essayli, speaking to Fox News Sunday, said that Zhang was a naturalized U.S. citizen.“She was conducting surveillance on behalf of the Chinese government," Essayli told Fox News. “And she was spying on a relative of the President of Taiwan here in the U.S.”Essayli, in his X post, added that Zhang “used tradecraft to avoid detection” and that “she never notified the Attorney General she was acting for a foreign government.” Under federal law, those who act as agents for other nations without prior notification to the U.S. Attorney General may face up to 10 years in prison, fines, or both.Zhang and another unnamed individual allegedly traveled from Las Vegas to Seattle around Sept. 1, 2025. The two then rented a black SUV and headed to the home of the victim they later surveilled. The complaint alleged that a home security camera near the victim’s house recorded Zhang and the individual “appearing to film” the victim and his family.The complaint does not name the victim, but CBS News reported, citing unidentified law enforcement sources, that the target was Ting-yu Lai, the son of Taiwanese President Lai. Zhang then allegedly messaged one of her Chinese government contacts, according to the complaint, where she sent: “Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one.” She then sent two license plate numbers, which the FBI agent found were both registered to the victim. The FBI agent wrote in the complaint that they were able to access details of Zhang’s messages following a search warrant on her iCloud account.“If [China] were to wish to obtain leverage over the President of Taiwan during any potential conflict, the location and pictures of the close relatives of a high-ranking Taiwanese government official, including pictures of their homes and cars, could be useful to [China],” the FBI special agent wrote.

items.title: Trump’s gains among Latino voters slip ahead of midterms
items.standfirst: New polls show Democrats ahead among Latino voters as Trump draws low marks on the economy and immigration enforcement.
items.content: President Donald Trump made major gains among Latino voters in 2024. Now, those same voters might cost Republicans control of Congress.Fifty-nine percent of Latino registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress, compared with 35% who favor Republican control, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll released Sunday. That 24-point gap for Democrats is twice the party’s lead compared to the September 2024 version of the poll.A separate CBS News/YouGov poll released Sunday also found Democrats ahead among Hispanic likely voters, with 60% backing a Democratic House candidate and 39% supporting a Republican.The findings threaten gains the GOP made in 2024, when Trump narrowed Democrats’ long-standing advantage among Latino voters. A POLITICO analysis of that year’s election results found that Trump improved his vote share by an average of more than 6 percentage points in majority-Hispanic counties, compared with 2020.With the midterms approaching, Republicans have made those gains central to their push to maintain control of the House. When Texas Republicans revealed their redistricting proposal last year, four of the five potential GOP pickup opportunities were in majority-Hispanic districts.Meanwhile, Trump’s overall approval rating among Latino registered voters stands at just 27% in the NBC/Telemundo poll, while 69% disapprove. On the economy specifically, 74% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump’s handling, while 78% disapprove of how he’s dealt with cost-of-living concerns.Nearly two-thirds, 65%, say Trump’s policies have hurt economic conditions. Inflation and cost of living rank as the most important issues facing the country for 33% of respondents, followed by government corruption at 22%. Another 10% named jobs and the economy.Economic frustration helped drive Latino voters toward Trump in 2024, with Democrats across the country suggesting in the aftermath of his victory that he was better able to connect with the voting bloc on financial issues.But now, Latino voters seem to favor Democrats over Republicans on the economy, 48% to 27%, and the cost of living, 45% compared to 26%.The war with Iran, now in its seventh month, is also weighing on voters’ perceptions of energy costs. In September, the average price of diesel hit a record $6.53, according to AAA.In the CBS survey, 91% of Hispanic registered voters attributed rising U.S. oil and gas prices to the conflict.Trump’s immigration crackdown is also putting vulnerable Republicans on the defensive. Rep. María Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) released an ad in English and Spanish criticizing the administration for going “too far” on immigration and saying Hispanics who backed Trump in 2024 feel “betrayed.”In the days immediately following her ad, Trump told reporters that he still supported Salazar. “I’m very strong on the borders — and she isn’t,” Trump said. But the president later reposted a flurry of social media messages criticizing Salazar on Truth Social, including one calling for the Florida Republican’s replacement ahead of the midterms.In the NBC/Telemundo poll, 67% of Latino voters say Trump’s immigration enforcement has gone too far, compared with 22% who say he has taken the right approach.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Dissatisfaction with Trump and Republicans has not translated into broadly positive views of Democrats. According to the NBC poll, Latino voters remain nearly evenly divided on the Democratic Party, with 41% viewing it positively and 42% negatively. Negative views of the GOP, meanwhile, have climbed to 62%, up from 46% in September 2024.The NBC/Telemundo survey of 800 Latino registered voters was conducted Sept. 21-28 and has a margin of error of ±3.46%. The CBS/YouGov survey of 2,166 adults was conducted Sept. 30-Oct. 2, with a margin of error of ±2.5 points.

items.title: Cornell President Vows ‘Serious Look’ at Campus Fraternities Amid Sexual Assault Allegations
items.standfirst: A civil lawsuit alleging gang rape at Cornell has led the university to promise a "serious look" at its fraternities.
items.content: Students walk past Cornell Police headquarters on the Cornell University campus in Ithaca, New York, on Sept. 30, 2026. —Spencer Platt—Getty ImagesCornell University is examining its fraternities and sororities after allegations of gang rape prompted concerns about accountability for sexual assault on college campuses.The university’s President Michael Kotlikoff said on Saturday in a video message to the university community that the school would take “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life” among other steps aimed at creating a safer campus environment.“At their best, these organizations can provide ​students with friendship, belonging, mentorship and a powerful sense of community,” Kotlikoff said. “But being part of ​a group can never diminish individual responsibility.”Kotlikoff said the university would seek input from students, alumni, and other community members about how to “preserve what is valuable about Greek life while strengthening individual accountability, transparency and a culture in ​which every member understands their responsibility to protect the safety and well-being of others.”The message comes on the heels of a civil lawsuit filed last month against Cornell and seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity. The plaintiff, anonymized as “Jane Doe,” alleged she was sexually assaulted and pressured to take drugs and alcohol on the night of Oct. 19, 2024, and that the university failed to protect her and mishandled its response. The lawsuit names seven current and former students as defendants, all of whom have denied any wrongdoing.The lawsuit has triggered renewed criticism of the handling of the allegations by the university and local authorities, who declined to pursue criminal charges at the time. On Thursday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, appointed the state’s Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor of the case, citing a loss of confidence in the local prosecutor’s ability to oversee it. New York lawmakers also said they were reviewing the state’s legal definition of consent while voluntarily intoxicated.Read More: The System That Failed Cornell’s Jane DoeKotlikoff was not among the administrators present at a university town hall on Thursday, where students, faculty, and alumni called for stronger action against campus sexual assault. The public meeting was led by the university’s student government. Some students shared their own stories of sexual harassment and assault.“I am also speaking as Jane Doe,” one student said at the forum.In a statement last week, Cornell defended its initial handling of the allegations and said it complied with university policies and Title IX. The university banned the Chi Phi fraternity from campus and launched a Title IX investigation in 2025, which resulted in a range of disciplinary measures for the seven members implicated.“We ​don’t have all the ⁠answers,” Kotlikoff said Saturday. “But we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”Jane Doe faces threats of doxxing, harm to drop lawsuitThomas Giuffra, the attorney representing Doe, told CNN on Sunday that people have threatened to harm her if she does not withdraw her civil lawsuit. Giuffra said there have also been multiple attempts to doxx Doe, which has resulted in at least three other women being mistakenly identified as her.“She’s received multiple threats, and women who aren’t even Jane Doe have received threats,” Giuffra said. “The threats, the abuse to protect what’s going on, the status quo, these guys are disgusting.”Ann Olivarius, a civil rights attorney and a plaintiff in the landmark Title IX sexual harassment case Alexander v. Yale (1977), told TIME last week that the backlash against Doe could deter sexual assault survivors from coming forward to make a report.That backlash has also prompted an outpouring of solidarity, with thousands of people posting #IamJaneDoe on social media. The posts are an effort to counter attempts to doxx Doe, but they have also become a way for survivors to share their own experiences of sexual assault.Lawsuit raises accountability concernsThe lawsuit has brought scrutiny to the university’s Title IX process, especially over its claim that some of the alleged perpetrators were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate” their disciplinary sentences by writing essays. Cornell said that nobody was allowed to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.After Doe reported the case in November 2024, Cornell conducted a closed proceeding by a three-member panel, which met on Zoom over 12 days in May 2025, the New York Times reported, citing records gathered by Cornell investigators. Individual sanctions and the reasoning behind them had not been publicly disclosed.According to discipline summaries obtained by the Times, the panel, which enforces federal civil rights at Cornell, did not conclude that Doe was sexually assaulted by all the men accused. Two of the fraternity members were found responsible for sexual assault and expelled. A third, who had graduated at the time of the ruling, was issued a persona non grata order barring him from campus for three years. Two others were suspended, given disciplinary probation, and required to study sexual harassment and write reflection papers. The remaining two, who were accused of being among the men that entered the room after reading a Snapchat message to the Chi Phi group chat encouraging others to join the alleged assault but were not accused of assaulting Doe themselves, were required to write reflection papers and attend trainings on sexual harassment, social media use, and bystander intervention. They were also barred from contacting Doe. None of the men has been criminally charged in connection with the allegations.Chi Phi’s Cornell chapter was suspended in 2024, and it remains barred from campus.Doe’s attorney as well as members of the Cornell community and the public have decried what they see as a lack of accountability for the alleged perpetrators. Doe ultimately withdrew from the university amid what the lawsuit described was a lack of institutional support. “With the exception of two of these men, all of them will be able to graduate with a Cornell diploma and live their lives reaping the benefits of this coveted degree,” Giuffra told the Times. “In contrast, as of today, it is doubtful whether Ms. Doe will even graduate college or ever live a normal life due to what these men did to her.”Some have also described the case as an indictment of Greek life culture. A 2021 study that followed 772 men through their first two years of college found that fraternity membership was associated with subsequent self-reported sexual aggression. Survivor advocates have also argued that fraternity environments can enable sexual assault.Giuffra told CNN that he has heard from people across the country about their own experiences of campus sexual assault since the lawsuit was filed. “This isn’t just a Cornell problem. This is a college-wide problem,” he said.Multiple universities, including Cornell, have suspended Greek life activities following sexual assault reports. In November 2022, Cornell temporarily suspended all fraternity parties and social events for the remainder of the fall semester after reports of four drugging incidents and a sexual assault.Some institutions have also permanently banned fraternal organizations. Swarthmore College banned fraternities and sororities in 2019 after student protests over leaked fraternity documents that contained racist and homophobic language and jokes about sexual assault. The college’s two fraternities had already voted to disband.Criminal investigation reopenedThe case has also drawn scrutiny to the Tompkins County District Attorney’s decision not to prosecute in 2024. The District Attorney, Matthew Van Houten, said last week he would review the case, but defended his initial decision, arguing that Doe’s sworn statement to police did not allege criminality. Under New York state law, if you choose to drink or take drugs to the point of becoming incapacitated, you can still be legally considered able to consent to sex.Critics have questioned Cornell police’s handling of Doe’s account. Cornell police appeared to have omitted Doe’s explicit assertion that she was raped from her six-page sworn statement, which was shared with prosecutors. Van Houten said his office did not receive the police interview transcript, in which Doe said, “I can say with 100% confidence I was raped.” Campus police later informed the prosecutor’s office of new interviews with witnesses after investigating anonymous tips, but prosecutors declined to review the additional evidence.On Friday, Hochul criticized prosecutors for relying on an incomplete account, asking: “In what world does the district attorney not even interview her, or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?”“This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable. And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her,” Hochul said.The governor also said she supports proposals to amend the so-called “voluntary intoxication loophole” in New York’s rape law. “If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape, period,” she said.The day before, Hochul appointed James, a Democrat, as special prosecutor.James had earlier posted on social media that what Doe had endured was “horrific and unacceptable,” raising questions from critics about her impartiality. James, who had already opened a review into Cornell’s response to the allegations, has pledged to conduct an investigation based on fact and the law.“We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions,” James said on Friday. “I know that you want answers. I do too. A comprehensive investigation of this nature takes time, but my office is committed to seeing it through.”President Donald Trump criticized the appointment, calling James a “corrupt person.”Trump has publicly feuded with James since she brought a civil fraud case against him and his family in 2022. The New York Supreme Court in September 2023 found Trump liable for fraud. An appeals court later upheld the fraud finding but overturned the financial penalty, which had grown to more than $500 million with interest.James was charged with mortgage fraud by the Justice Department last year, but a judge dismissed the case and two grand juries rejected subsequent attempts to indict her. James denies the allegations.Both James and Hochul have also criticized Trump over allegations of sexual misconduct and misogyny. In 2016, James, then New York City’s public advocate, condemned Trump’s “disgusting record of sexual misconduct.” In January 2024, months after a civil jury found Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming E. Jean Carroll, Hochul signed a bill expanding the legal definition of rape to include nonconsensual vaginal, oral, and anal sexual acts. Trump has dropped his challenge to the $5 million damages awarded to Carroll, but continues to contest a separate $83 million defamation award. The Justice Department opened a criminal investigation into Carroll in May over whether she committed perjury.Asked about the Cornell allegations on Thursday, Trump said he knew little about the case but expressed confidence that the university would respond appropriately. In later social media posts and comments to reporters, however, he cast doubt on whether James would conduct a fair investigation.“I feel ⁠badly for ​whoever she’s looking at,” Trump told reporters on Friday, “because they won’t get a fair shake.”
